lessons.title: Why Skew Exists: Leverage, Fear, and Jump Risk

children.text: Chapter 1 showed you the shape: in the illustrative Nifty smile you built, a strike 800 points below spot priced in 16.8% IV while the equidistant strike above spot priced in only 14.9%, a gap of about 1.9 volatility points for options the same distance from the money. Black-Scholes has no explanation for that. The model assumes one constant volatility for every strike. The market disagrees, consistently, every single day, on every major index. This lesson is about why.

body.text: Volatility skew is not a pricing error. It is the market charging three distinct premiums at once: for the mechanical fact that falling prices make companies riskier, for the real possibility of a sudden crash that a smooth model cannot capture, and for structural demand from hedgers who buy downside protection with almost no natural sellers on the other side.

markDefs.definition: The empirical observation, documented by Fischer Black in 1976, that a stock's realized volatility tends to rise after its price falls and fall after its price rises, a negative correlation between returns and subsequent volatility.

children.text: gives a clean mechanical story. A firm carries a mostly fixed amount of debt. If its stock price falls, the same debt load now sits against a smaller equity cushion, so the debt-to-equity ratio rises. Equity in a more indebted firm is a riskier, more volatile claim on the business, because equity holders absorb losses first. A falling stock price therefore mechanically raises the volatility of that stock going forward, and option markets, anticipating this, price higher IV at lower strikes.

body.text: This explanation works cleanly for a single stock. It does not translate directly to Nifty. An index is not one company with a balance sheet and a debt-to-equity ratio, it is fifty companies with different leverage profiles that rarely all re-rate their risk in the same direction at once. The leverage effect matters more for understanding why a specific single-name's skew looks the way it does than for explaining the skew you see on Nifty or Bank Nifty, where the next two explanations carry more of the weight.

children.text: Explanation Two: The Crash Risk Premium

Black-Scholes assumes the underlying moves continuously, in infinitesimally small steps, with no sudden jumps. Real markets do not behave that way, and index option markets learned this lesson at a specific, dated moment.

body.title: How Black Monday Reshaped the Smile

events.title: A roughly flat smile
events.description: US equity index option IV was documented as broadly similar across strikes, close to the single constant-volatility assumption Black-Scholes makes.

events.title: Black Monday
events.description: The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell about 22.6% in a single session, the largest one-day percentage decline in its history, with no comparable single news event fully explaining a move of that size.

events.title: A persistent skew emerges
events.description: OTM index put IV rose relative to OTM call IV and has stayed structurally elevated ever since. The market had just learned that a fast, discontinuous, multi-standard-deviation crash was a real possibility, not a theoretical curiosity, and it never fully unpriced that lesson.

markDefs.definition: A sudden, discontinuous price move that a continuous-diffusion model like Black-Scholes cannot represent. Jump-diffusion models, first formalized by Robert Merton in 1976, add a jump component on top of continuous diffusion specifically to price this risk.

children.text: A model that cannot represent a

cannot price the risk of one either, unless it cheats by raising the volatility input specifically where the jump risk concentrates, which is on the downside for equity indices. Feed the market's true crash-inclusive view of the world into a Black-Scholes solver and the only way it can express extra downside danger is a higher sigma at low strikes. That forced workaround is, mechanically, exactly what a volatility skew is. The index case matters more here than the single-stock case: a systemic crash, a war, a sovereign crisis, a liquidity freeze, hits every constituent of Nifty at once, so index puts carry a concentrated bet on exactly that undiversifiable, all-at-once risk.
Explanation Three: Structural Supply and Demand

The first two explanations describe why buyers should rationally pay more for downside protection. The third explains why sellers do not compete that premium away. On any given day, there is a large, persistent, largely one-directional flow of institutions wanting to buy OTM index puts, and comparatively few natural sellers willing to underwrite that risk cheaply.

body.title: Who is on each side of the skew

columns.label: Put side: mostly buying pressure
points: Mutual funds and insurers hedging equity book drawdowns ahead of known events
FPIs hedging India exposure without unwinding cash equity positions
Retail and prop desks buying protective puts or put spreads
Structured products that embed a long-put payoff for the issuer's client
Few natural sellers willing to be permanently short crash insurance at a cheap price

columns.label: Call side: mostly selling pressure
points: Covered call writing against existing long equity or index positions
Yield-enhancement structured notes that sell upside in exchange for a coupon
Retail call writers collecting premium against long cash positions
Fewer buyers willing to pay up heavily for unlimited upside participation
This selling pressure caps how expensive OTM call IV can get, unlike the put side

body.text: This is why the skew is asymmetric rather than a symmetric smile. If fear and hedging demand pushed prices around evenly on both wings, you would see a smile. Because the demand for protection concentrates almost entirely on the downside, with the upside instead facing sellers, not buyers, the curve gets pulled into a smirk. Watch this flow intensify around scheduled Indian risk events, the Union Budget, an RBI policy day, a large index rebalancing, when institutional put buying for tactical protection visibly steepens the skew in the days beforehand.

body.title: Attributing the driver
body.question: A single mid-cap stock's OTM put IV rises sharply relative to its OTM call IV after a poor quarterly result that materially increases its reported debt-to-equity ratio, with no broader market stress. Which explanation is the primary driver here?
options: Structural index-hedging flow from mutual funds
A change in NSE's strike interval convention
body.explanation: A single-name event that specifically raises one company's leverage, with no broader market stress and no systemic hedging flow involved, is the textbook case for the leverage effect: a smaller equity cushion against the same debt makes the equity itself riskier, and OTM puts on that stock re-rate accordingly. Crash risk premium and structural hedging flow are index-level, cross-sectional explanations, not single-name balance sheet ones.

body.title: Skew steepening into a known event
body.scenario: Three trading days before a Union Budget announcement, you notice the 25-delta put on the Nifty monthly expiry has gained about 2.5 volatility points relative to the ATM strike, while the 25-delta call has barely moved. Realized volatility over the past week has been unremarkable. A junior colleague argues this must mean the market suddenly believes leverage across Nifty's constituents has deteriorated.
body.prompt: Is the leverage-effect explanation the right one here? What is actually driving this move, and how would you expect it to unwind?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The leverage effect is the wrong lens for this move. Nifty is not a single balance sheet, and nothing in the scenario describes a broad, sudden deterioration in the debt-to-equity ratios of fifty different constituent companies in three days.
2. The pattern, put-side IV rising sharply while call-side IV barely moves and realized vol stays calm, is the signature of structural hedging demand ahead of a known, dated event: institutions buying downside protection specifically because the Budget can move the market sharply in either direction, and puts are the standard hedge.
3. This is a crash-risk and supply-demand story, not a leverage story. The market is not saying 'companies are more indebted now,' it is saying 'a scheduled event with genuine two-sided uncertainty is imminent, and there are more buyers of downside insurance than sellers into it.'
4. Expect this event-driven steepening to partially or fully unwind quickly once the Budget passes without a crash-sized surprise, since the specific uncertainty that justified the extra put premium has resolved. This unwind is exactly the term-structure and event-vol behavior covered in Chapter 3.
5. If a desk had sold that elevated put skew into the event expecting reversion and the event genuinely produced a large adverse move, the position would have been on the wrong side of exactly the risk the skew was pricing, which is the core hazard of selling event-driven skew mechanically without a view on the event itself.

cards.definition: A falling stock price raises a firm's debt-to-equity ratio, making its equity riskier and raising expected future volatility. Explains single-name skew better than index skew.
The extra IV a continuous-diffusion model like Black-Scholes must embed at low strikes to compensate for the real possibility of a sudden, discontinuous crash it cannot otherwise represent.
A model family, formalized by Merton in 1976, that adds a discrete jump component on top of continuous price diffusion to explicitly price crash risk.
The persistent, largely one-directional demand from institutions to buy OTM index puts for portfolio protection, with comparatively few natural sellers, that keeps put-side IV structurally elevated.
The single trading day, a roughly 22.6% Dow decline, after which equity index options permanently shifted from a broadly flat smile to a persistent negative skew.

points: Skew is not mispricing. It reflects three real, distinct premiums the market charges: the leverage effect, a crash risk premium a continuous model cannot otherwise represent, and structural hedging demand with few natural counterparties.
The leverage effect explains single-stock skew well but only weakly explains index skew, since an index is not one company with a single balance sheet.

Black Monday, 19 October 1987, marks the historical point after which equity index option markets moved from a roughly flat smile to a persistent, structurally negative skew that has never fully gone away.

Put-side IV is pushed up mainly by buying pressure from hedgers; call-side IV is capped by selling pressure from covered-call and yield-enhancement flow. That asymmetry in who is on each side is what turns a symmetric smile into a lopsided smirk.

Skew visibly steepens ahead of known, dated risk events, such as the Union Budget or an RBI policy day, as hedging demand concentrates, and typically partially unwinds once the event passes without a large surprise.

Correctly attributing a skew move to the right one of these three explanations, rather than defaulting to one story, is a prerequisite for the quantified skew metrics and trading structures in the rest of this chapter.
